rationale: Demand is A-grade (permit open data) but every fee is hypothesized. Market is shrinking (48.5k to 32k permits) and relationship-locked (top 10 = 46%). Capital is small, but hiring an expediter on day one adds salary burn. The ceiling is local and Chicago-only. Base case is about $75-125k.
red_flags: private fee levels MISSING; $500-3,000 is E

rationale: Mandated recurring work with repair pull-through and strong consolidator exit value. But the founder must hire a scarce DCP plus NICET III inspectors before revenue, and installers hold their installed base. Economics are APi incumbent figures plus E pricing. Year-3 range of $20-250k shows how uncertain it is.
red_flags: incumbent APi margins used as proxy

rationale: Bulky commodity sold against Sysco, WebstaurantStore and Restaurant Depot. The record's own estimate is a 3-6% operating margin on stock goods. Custom print is the only wedge, and it is lumpy, deposit-heavy and copied by online printers. Restaurant churn and bad debt add risk. Base case is roughly $40-60k.

No evidence that subs buy outsourced closeout; the main competitor is in-house staff. Asset-light with real AI document-matching leverage, but buyers can adopt the same AI or Procore tools. Receivables are slow (pay-when-paid), and the stated ceiling is $10k/mo.

NFPA 96 makes this mandated, frequent work with reachable buyers and no state license. It is a low-barrier, price-shopped field with franchises and many independents. Night-crew quality and fire-loss liability are the main risks. Pricing is analyst-estimated. A sound but ordinary route business, about $100k base with 2-3 crews.

PPE consumables run straight into Grainger, Fastenal and Amazon. The services wedge (fit testing, calibration) is real but small-ticket and capacity-bound. Ergodyne's $75k minimum shows the supplier hurdle. Inventory, rental fleet and slow contractor receivables pull ROIC down. Margins come from incumbents.

Plausible, repeatable truck-and-tech units with short sales cycles and no license identified. But the only source is a permit-volume proxy; pricing and competition are both hypothesized. A strong national scanning player exists, and strike liability is real. Possibly under-sold, but evidence is weak.

Mandated testing plus monitoring income builds a valuable, sticky base, and POTS sunsets create switching events. However, the IDFPR alarm-contractor license may need 3 years of experience or a hired licensee. Income builds slowly (profit in 24 months) and the field is crowded with consolidators.

Margin is documented by ASI (37%), supplier access is open, and it needs almost no capital. But the field is extremely crowded with no barriers, demand is discretionary marketing spend, and owner income depends on founder or rep selling volume. The $16M operator is a testimonial (D). The $500k ceiling is a stretch.

Code-required niche where certification can build credibility. But the founder has no trade background, union jurisdiction is unverified, and GC prequal and bidding apply. Retainage and pay-when-paid tie up $250-400k at scale. The 18% margin is the Census average for incumbents, not new entrants.

Lumpy, equipment-heavy niche: canine and heat-treatment gear. Needs a licensed pest-control business and certified technician. Economics are thin and unsourced; pricing is analyst-estimated. Proactive hotel inspection demand is assumed, and the Chicago ordinance was not verified.

Small, relationship-driven dealer and consultant community; top lines are held by established agencies. The newcomer has no lines and no credibility. Commission rate is MISSING, profitability takes 24 months, and income depends on restaurant capex. The year-3 low of $0 is realistic.

Low barriers, price-driven GC buying, and work tied to a weakening construction cycle (completions down 10%). Weekly payroll against net-45-60 pay-when-paid creates a negative cash cycle. Delegable labor, but low and local profit. Pricing is MISSING.

Mandated, recurring FOG pumping with limited disposal access acting as a moat. But it needs a $100k+ vacuum truck, CDL labor and hauler permits (unverified). Economics are analyst estimates, and the record itself puts ROIC at 25-90%. Disposal fees are MISSING.

Very lumpy commission income on 6-18-month capex cycles; the $0 low case is realistic. Depends on foreign principals and is exposed to tariffs. Personal relationships and engineering credibility make it hard to delegate. Commission rates are members-only and MISSING.

Real ticket data (median $22k) and a Census margin proxy. Deposits help cash. Capable hard-selling entrants do build $1-3M roofers. But competition is extreme, lead costs are MISSING, and the licence requires passing the qualifying-party exam. The Roofing Act sunset is unresolved.

Healthcare damper testing is code- and accreditation-driven with little competition. But no spend data was gathered, cycles are multi-year and lumpy, institutional buyers are slow, and receivables run net-45/90. Pricing is analyst-estimated. Better as a bundle with fire-door inspection than standalone.

Pure hardware resale at single-digit to low-teen margins, against CDW and Amazon. The record admits the entry strategy is weak and profit lives in managed services. Even ePlus earns 6.8% operating at scale. There is little reason to pursue it standalone.

High gross margin, deposit-funded, light licensing (Chicago Class E). But demand is discretionary and seasonal in Chicago, with no repeat business. Lead competition from franchises is heavy. The margin is a flooring-wide Census proxy; coating-specific economics and lead costs are MISSING.

Simple, delegable recurring route with low capital. But it has low price points, HVAC contractors can bundle filters into their own maintenance, and there is no demand or pricing evidence. Roof-safety exposure. Largely duplicates WS16-024.

No category is identified. Inventory sits in a long negative cash cycle (prepay, 60-120 days in transit, then net-30/60), and the dealer network must be built from scratch. Exposed to tariffs and FX, and the principal can pull exclusivity once the market is built. The $1M ceiling claim is unsupported.

High-ticket, urgent need-driven jobs in a basement-heavy metro, with deposits. But Chicago mason and plumbing licence boundaries for drain-tile and sump work are unresolved. Ad competition is high and warranty liability lingers. Pricing and spend are hypothesized; the permit proxy is weak.

Annual inspection is a recommended practice, not a clear mandate, with repair and replacement pull-through. Chains route work through national facility-management providers, and manufacturer dealer lock-out on parts is a real risk. No spend data; certification prerequisites are unverified.

Major brands use captive distribution (SalonCentric, CosmoProf), leaving only indie brands that get acquired and pulled. The founder has no industry fit and there is no market data. The year-3 range of $0-80k doesn't support the $250k ceiling.

Baseline remodeler: Census proxy (13.5% operating margin, $678k average receipts) implies a modest owner income. Demand is discretionary and housing-weak, with extreme competition and no wedge. Deposits help cash and licensing is easy. Typical small business at best.

Mandated demand, but OEM oligopoly, union licensed mechanics, proprietary parts and $100-300k payroll before multi-year contracts. The record itself says there is no credible entry. Contribution economics are MISSING.

Chicago's large industrial market creates observable triggers (leases, closures). Deposit-funded, drop-shipped projects keep capital light, and used rack plus inspections add margin and recurrence. Risks: cyclical, lumpy, dealer criteria MISSING, margins proxied by Census. Fits a technical, sales-willing founder.

Low capital, paid at closing, with deadline-driven referrals from inspectors. The IEMA licence is obtainable but details are MISSING, and Chicago electrical rules limit fan wiring. Volume is tied to home sales at 7%+ rates, and prevalence and competitor counts are MISSING. Solid small business with a modest ceiling.

Capital-intensive sweeper trucks for modest monthly contracts, with net-30/60 property-manager receivables. Delegable driver work. No pricing or competition data. Winter overlaps with snow work in a way that could help or hurt.

Service contracts and parts are recurring. But big brands sell direct in large metros, dealer territories may be taken, and rental fleet plus parts inventory raise capital. Profitability takes 24 months. No margin evidence.

Fits the founder's video and IoT skills, and AI detection genuinely cuts monitoring labor. But national players already use AI, the rental comps come from different equipment categories, and per-unit returns (revenue about 50% of unit cost) imply ROIC near 30-60%. Alarm-licence applicability and BIPA are open questions. Tied to the construction cycle.

Easy to start: tiny capital, card-on-file billing, door-to-door sales, highly delegable. But small tickets, Chicago winters and a low ceiling (record says $10k/mo) cap profit. ROIC is very high, but absolute FCF falls short of mandate scale.

Data-center build-out supports demand, and same-day custom fiber assemblies are a real wedge. But commodity cable competes with WESCO and Graybar, supplier criteria are unchecked, and connector inventory plus 45-60+ day contractor receivables weigh on cash. Entrant margins E.

4-5 month season with idle capital the rest of the year, mild-winter risk, and fuel/CO safety issues. Competes with national rental firms that bundle heat. The record's own ceiling is $5k/mo. Poor on every economic axis.

OSHA anchorage certification gives a mandate basis, but enforcement is weak. Certification needs a PE partner, and liability if an anchor fails is serious. Niche ceiling. No spend, pricing or competitor data.

Same business as WS05-014, with slightly better category evidence (open supplier base, Census GM). Delegable recurring route with low capital. But HVAC contractors bundle filters, route pricing is unknown, and route density takes time to build. The $500k ceiling is optimistic.

Paid upfront, cheap to start, and AI report drafting is a real cost lever. But agent referrals gate demand, volume moves with a slow housing market, competition is high, and multi-inspector margins are 15-25%. The Act sunsets in 2027 (status unverified).

Customer-funded and highly delegable, with identifiable buyers and a recurring, essential service. The healthcare protocol wedge is modest. CBP gives counts and payroll only; the claimed 15-25% operating margin and $1M ceiling are optimistic (about 10-15% typical). Labor turnover is the core risk.

Incumbent data (Pool, SiteOne, Core & Main) shows deep inventory needs and slow turns. Over $150k must go in before the first sale, key lines are allocated to incumbents, and consolidators compete hard. The record admits there is no credible entry.

Counter-cyclical sourcing is a sensible idea, and AI listing helps. But supply is unreliable, goods are bulky with warehouse costs, dead stock is a risk, and the ceiling is local ($10k/mo stated). Resale volumes and surplus pricing are MISSING.
Low-capital subcontract niche for janitorial firms, with summer school peaks. Primes can bring the work in-house. Low ceiling, no pricing data. Better as a janitorial add-on than standalone.

Brands are easy to sign, but they churn and fail, retail buyers gate access, and the founder has no category-management fit. Retainers are assumed and commissions are low single digits. The $0 low case is realistic.

Recurring fees taken from collected rent, durable rental demand, and a density moat over time. But it needs a broker licence plus a hired managing broker, and reaching 300 doors by year 3 is optimistic. Fee norms are MISSING. Operating load is heavy and escrow errors carry legal risk.

Middleman layer over mandated work, at a low $50-200 per building per month. Vendors can bypass it, and clients can 'just call vendors'. Contracting for licensed services risks unlicensed practice. AI document parsing is useful but doesn't fix weak willingness to pay. Better as a lead engine.

Exclusive OEM territories (Watsco 10-K) lock major lines to incumbents, and specifiers are loyal. 6-24 month cycles, profitability at 30 months, and buy-sell retainage exposure. The founder has a mechanical-engineering gap. Leftover minor lines only.

Spread on master leases carries hidden fixed-rent liability, and vacancy wipes out a thin $300-1,000/unit-month contribution. Travel-nurse demand is softening, landlord consent is unverified, and demand data is MISSING. Scaling multiplies lease risk.

Weekly subscription route that bundles naturally with hood cleaning. But it needs a filter pool plus a wash facility with wastewater permits. No demand or pricing evidence; adoption is the key unknown.
Drop-ship removes inventory, but this is commodity office and breakroom supply against Amazon and Staples at 15-28% GM. Wholesaler minimums can close the account within 6 months. Ceiling is $10k/mo.

Illinois treats a pattern of wholesaling as brokerage, so a licence is required. Seller acquisition relies on aggressive mail and cold calling to distressed owners (TCPA and consumer-protection risk). Competition is extreme, and the record itself recommends rejection.
Seasonal in Chicago, with small-ticket route work, high competition and a $10k/mo ceiling. Stormwater and wastewater rules apply. Delegable and cheap, but not mandate-scale.

Rates, ticket and contribution are all MISSING. Needs Medicare portable X-ray supplier certification, IEMA registration, rad techs and $60-200k before revenue at month 9, against entrenched SNF incumbents. Exposed to reimbursement cuts.

Buyers actively search during impairments, and the low-skill pool is easy to delegate. But demand is occasional and lumpy, and weekly payroll runs against net-30 receivables. Possible private-security licensing (IDFPR, 3 years' experience) is unresolved. Demand volume is MISSING.
